extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, copyeditors, and publishers preparing manuscripts for scholarly or formal publication (University of Chicago Press style)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for spelling choices and punctuation usage applicable to manuscripts for scholarly publication, covering -ise/-ize terminations, periods, commas, colons, semicolons, dashes, parentheses, brackets, ellipses, hyphens, apostrophes, and related typographic conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate between the terminations -ise and -ize
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between the terminations -ise and -ize as follows: provide explicit lists of words that should be spelled with -ise and those that should be spelled with -ize {-yze}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SPELL WITH -ise: advertise, comprise, enterprise, premise, advise, affranchise, compromise, demise, excise, exercise, reprise, revise, appraise, apprise (to inform), despise, devise, disfranchise, exorcise, franchise, improvise, rise, supervise, surmise, arise, disguise, incise, surprise, chastise, circumcise, emprise, enfranchise, manuprise, merchandise. SPELL WITH -ize {-yze}: aggrandize, agonize, analyze, autolyze, baptize, brutalize, civilize, classicize, colonize, energize, epitomize, equalize, anatomize, canonize, criticize, eulogize, anglicize, apologize, apostrophize, apprize (to appraise), authorize, catechize, catholicize, cauterize, centralize, characterize, christianize, crystallize, demoralize, deputize, dogmatize, economize, emphasize, evangelize, extemporize, familiarize, fertilize, fossilize, fraternize, galvanize, methodize, polarize, stigmatize, generalize, minimize, professionalize, subsidize, gormandize, modernize, protestantize, summarize, harmonize, monopolize, pulverize, syllogize, hellenize, moralize, realize, symbolize, humanize, nationalize, recognize, sympathize, immortalize, naturalize, reorganize, tantalize, italicize, neutralize, revolutionize, temporize, jeopardize, organize, satirize, tranquilize, legalize, ostracize, scandalize, tyrannize, liberalize, oxidize, scrutinize, utilize, localize, paralyze, signalize, vaporize, magnetize, particularize, solemnize, visualize, manumize, pasteurize, soliloquize, vitalize, memorialize, patronize, specialize, vocalize, mesmerize, philosophize, spiritualize, vulgarize, metamorphize, plagiarize, standardize, vulg arize (etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Typography of punctuation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: All punctuation marks should be printed in the same style or font of type as the word or letter immediately preceding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'With the cry of Banzai!' the punctuation should match preceding word style; same rule applies to letters and numerals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period indicates sentence end
rubrics_metrics.description: A period is used to indicate the end of a complete sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (See related rules about placement in quotations, abbreviations, and running heads.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Period after abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a period after all abbreviations, except in cases where a mechanical necessity compels the omission of a letter or letters in the middle of a word for which there is no recognized abbreviated form; such omission is indicated by an apostrophe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat metric symbols as abbreviations (e.g., 10 mm.), but not chemical symbols (Fe), nor 'per cent', nor book format abbreviations (4to, 8vo). Note journal-specific exceptions (Astrophysical Journal, Botanical Gazette) and special forms like m'f'g pl't (= manufacturing plant).

rubrics_metrics.name: No period after certain recognized abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a period in technical matter after recognized abbreviations for linguistic epochs or after initials of well-known publications, nor after MS (= manuscript).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: IE (= Indo-European), OE (= Old English), MHG (= Middle High German), AJSL (= American Journal of Semitic Languages and Literatures), ZAW, CIL. (See exceptions in other contexts.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No period after Roman numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use no period after Roman numerals, even if having the value of ordinals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vol. IV; Louis XVI was on the throne.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit period after certain headings and elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the period after running-heads, after centered headlines, after side-heads set in separate lines, after cut-in heads, after box-heads in tables, and after superscriptions and legends which do not form a complete sentence; also omit after date lines at top of communications and after signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (See rule 50 for explanation of running-heads etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Period placement with quotation marks and parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The period is placed inside the quotation marks; and inside parentheses when the matter enclosed is an independent sentence and forms no part of the preceding sentence; otherwise, outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as a rule without exception. Examples: Tennyson's 'In Memoriam.' Put the period inside the quotation marks. Put the period inside parentheses when the parenthetical is a full sentence; otherwise outside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclamation point usage and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclamation point is used to mark an outcry, or an emphatic or ironical utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the exclamation point inside quotation marks when part of the quotation; otherwise outside. Examples provided in rule 127 and 128.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogation point usage and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: The interrogation point is used to mark a query or to express a doubt; indirect questions should not be followed by an interrogation point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the interrogation point inside quotation marks only when it is part of the quotation. Example: 'Who is this?' Indirect question: He asked whether he was ill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon usage and functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The colon marks a discontinuity of grammatical construction greater than that indicated by the semicolon and less than that indicated by the period; commonly used (i) to emphasize a close connection between two complete clauses, (2) to separate a clause from an illustration or amplification, (3) to introduce a formal statement, an extract, a speech in dialogue, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before a quotation of a clause in the middle of a sentence use a comma. The colon often substitutes for 'namely', 'as follows', 'for instance' — follow with colon if what follows are grammatically complete clauses, otherwise use a comma. Put a colon after salutatory phrases in letters (My dear Mr. Brown:) and between chapter and verse in Scripture and between hours and minutes. Place colon outside quotation marks unless part of the quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A semicolon is used to mark the division of a sentence somewhat more independent than that marked by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use semicolons in complex enumerations where links contain commas or longer clauses; in Scripture references to separate passages containing chapters; place semicolon outside quotation marks unless part of quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma general principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma is used to indicate the smallest interruptions in continuity of thought or grammatical construction, marking what contributes to clearness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous specific uses and exceptions follow (see rules 142–162 for detailed comma guidance and examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma to separate proper nouns of different individuals/places
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate proper nouns belonging to different individuals or places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'To John, Smith was always kind'; 'To America, Europe awards the prize of mechanical skill.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before final 'and/or/nor' in lists (Oxford comma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma before 'and', 'or', and 'nor' connecting the last two links in a sequence of three or more; or before all links in longer series, or where each link consists of several words; always put a comma before 'etc.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tom, Dick, and Harry; either copper, silver, or gold. Exception: do not use where 'and' connects a brief, close-knit phrase: 'a man good and noble and true.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma with clauses introduced by conjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily put a comma before and after clauses introduced by conjunctions such as 'and', 'but', 'if', 'while', 'as', 'whereas', 'since', 'because', 'when', 'after', 'although' especially if a change of subject occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But omit when the preceding clause is not logically complete without them or in brief close-welded phrases (examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma after introductory connective adverbs/phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Words or phrases like 'now', 'then', 'however', 'indeed', 'therefore', 'moreover', 'furthermore', 'nevertheless', 'in fact', 'for example', etc., should be followed by a comma when standing at the beginning of a sentence or clause to introduce an inference or explanation, and should be placed between commas when wedged into the middle of a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use a comma with such words when connection is logically close and structurally smooth enough not to require a pause; e.g., 'Therefore I say unto you...' or 'He was perhaps thinking of the future.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before 'rather' in particular expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma is preferably omitted before 'rather' in expressions like 'measured in this way rather than by...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The time-value is to be measured in this way rather than by the time-equivalent of the strata.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma to separate identical or closely similar words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate two identical or closely similar words even if the sense or grammatical construction does not require such separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Whatever is, is good'; 'What he was, is not known.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma to set off complementary/qualifying adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: In adjectival phrases, a complementary, qualifying, delimiting, or antithetical adjective added to the main epithet preceding a noun should be preceded and followed by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This harsh, though perfectly logical, conclusion'; 'The most sensitive, if not the most elusive, part...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma to separate coordinate clauses governing a following word
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more coordinate clauses ending in a word governing or modifying another word in a following clause should be separated by commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a shallow body of water connected with, but well protected from, the open sea'; 'He was as tall as, though much younger than, his brother.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma between two numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate two numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'In 1905, 347 teachers attended the convention'; 'November I, 1905.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma to indicate omitted words
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma is employed to indicate the omission, for brevity or convenience, of a word or words the repetition of which is not essential to the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'In Illinois there are seventeen such institutions; in Ohio, twenty-two.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before brief direct quotations or maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: A brief direct quotation, maxim, or similar expression should be separated from the preceding part of the sentence by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'God said, Let there be light.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before 'of' with residence or position
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma before 'of' in connection with residence or position: Mr. and Mrs. Mclntyre, of Detroit, Mich.; President Hadley, of Yale University.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: when the place-name has practically become part of the person's name (Clement of Alexandria, Philip of Anjou).

rubrics_metrics.name: No comma between consecutive pages; use en-dash
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a comma between consecutive pages in literary references; use an en-dash instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: pp. 4, 7-8, 10; scriptural references may be treated as exceptions (Ezra 5:7-8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma after digits indicating thousands
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma after digits indicating thousands, except when used as a date or in a page-reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 1,276; 10,419; January, 1909; p. 2461. Note: some journals (Astrophysical Journal, Botanical Gazette) do not use a comma with four figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma between month and year
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate month and year by a comma: November, 1905; New Year's Day, 1906.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: Astrophysical Journal and Botanical Gazette do not use a comma between month and year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit comma in signatures and certain heading lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the comma in signatures and at the beginning of articles after an author's name followed by address, title, or position in a separate line, or after an address followed by a date line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate signature block formatting without commas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma always inside quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma is always placed inside the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 162.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophe for contractions and omitted figures
rubrics_metrics.description: An apostrophe is used to mark the omission of a letter or letters in the contraction of a word, or of figures in a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ne'er, don't, 'twas, 'takin' me 'at', m'f'g, the class of '96.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming the possessive case
rubrics_metrics.description: The possessive case of nouns, common and proper, is formed by the addition of an apostrophe, or apostrophe and s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a man's, horses' tails; Scott's Ivanhoe; Jones's farms; Themistocles' era; for appearance' sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural and possessive forms of numerals and rare coinages
rubrics_metrics.description: The plural of numerals and of rare or artificial noun-coinages is formed by the aid of an apostrophe and s; of proper nouns of more than one syllable ending in a sibilant, form plural by adding an apostrophe alone (monosyllabic proper names ending in a sibilant add es; others add s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in the 1900's; in two's and three's; the three R's; the Y.M.C.A.'s; 'all the Tommy Atkins' of England' (but: the Rosses and the Macdougals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash denotes sudden break/transition
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash is used to denote a sudden break, stop, or transition in a sentence, or an abrupt change in its construction, a long or significant pause, or an unexpected or epigrammatic turn of sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Do we — can we — send out educated boys and girls...' 'To be or not to be — that is the question.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dashes for independent parenthetical clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dashes (rarely parentheses) for parenthetical clauses which are both logically and structurally independent interpolations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate use of dashes for strong independent interpolations; see rule 167.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash to introduce emphasizing or explanatory clause repeating phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: A clause added to lend emphasis to, or to explain or expand, a word or phrase occurring in the main clause, which word or phrase is then repeated, should be introduced by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'To him they are more important as the sources for history — the history of events and ideas.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dash where 'namely' is implied
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a 'namely' is implied before a parenthetical or complementary clause, a dash should preferably be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'These discoveries — gunpowder, printing-press, compass, and telescope — were the weapons...' 'Here we are trenching upon another division of our field — the interpretation of New Testament books.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash precedes final summarizing clause
rubrics_metrics.description: In sentences broken up into clauses, the final — summarizing — clause should be preceded by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example demonstrates use in a list culminating in a summary clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash after a separate-line lead-in followed by paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: A word or phrase set in a separate line and succeeded by paragraphs, at the beginning of each of which it is implied, should be followed by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I recommend — 1. That we kill him. 2. That we flay him.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash for side-heads and headings
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash should be used in connection with side-heads, whether 'run in' or paragraphed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The language of the New Testament. — The lexicons of Grimm-Thayer...' Also use dashes for headings that introduce a block.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dash (en- or em-dash) in place of 'to' connecting ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a dash in place of the word 'to' connecting two words or numbers; distinguish en-dash and em-dash appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: May-July, 1906 (en-dash); May 1, 1905 — November 1, 1906 (em-dash); pp. 3-7 (en-dash). In connecting consecutive numbers, omit hundreds from the second number unless certain conditions apply; for B.C. dates always repeat hundreds. Note some journals vary in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash before references after a direct quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a dash precede the reference (author, title of work, or both) following a direct quotation consisting of at least one complete sentence, in footnotes or cited independently in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I felt an emotion of the moral sublime at beholding such an instance of civic heroism.' — Thirty Years, I, 379.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid combining dash with other punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash should not ordinarily be used in connection with any other point, except a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrect: 'Dear Sir: — I have the honor...' Correct: 'Dear Sir: I have the honor...' Also avoid constructions like 'This, — I say it with regret, — was...' (incorrect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses for enumerative markers and limited parentheticals
rubrics_metrics.description: Place between parentheses figures or letters used to mark divisions in enumerations run into the text; parentheses should not ordinarily be used for parenthetical clauses unless confusion might arise or the content is wholly irrelevant to the main argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parentheses for (i) enumerative markers; use rarely for parentheticals if dashes would suffice. Examples and recommended indentation schemes for multi-level enumerations are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brackets for editorial insertions and corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Brackets are used to inclose an explanation or note, to indicate an interpolation in a quotation, to rectify a mistake, to supply an omission, and for parentheses within parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: [This was written before... — Editor.], 'These [the free-silver Democrats] asserted...', correcting misprints within quotations, citation corrections, and nested parentheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brackets for 'To be continued' and similar notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'To be continued' at the end, and 'Continued from...' at the beginning of articles or chapters should be placed between brackets, centered, set in italics and in type reduced in size according to rules governing reductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: [Continued from p. 320] [To be concluded]

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses indicate omission and lacunae
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipses are used to indicate the omission, from a quotation, of one or more words not essential to the idea which it is desired to convey, and to indicate illegible words, mutilations, and other lacunae in a quoted document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For an ellipsis at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence use four periods separated by a space (en-quad) ordinarily, except in very narrow measures. If the preceding line ends in a point do not include it in the four. For omitted entire paragraphs or lines in poetry insert a full line of periods separated by em- or 2-em quads, but do not extend beyond the longest type-line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses treated as part of citation
rubrics_metrics.description: An ellipsis should be treated as a part of the citation and consequently should be enclosed in the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (See rule 181 and rule 178 [3] regarding quotations and editorial marks.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate line-break syllables and compound adjectives before nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is placed at the end of a line terminating with a syllable of a word carried to the next line and between many compound words. Hyphenate two or more words combined into one adjective preceding a noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: well-known author, first-class investment, better-trained teachers, high-school course, four-year-old boy. When components are set in capitals or one component contains more than one word, use an en-dash (FRANCO-PRUSSIAN WAR; New York–Chicago freight traffic). Do not hyphenate adverb + adjective combinations where the adverb ends in '-ly' or when the phrase follows the noun or qualifies a predicate (highly developed species; a man well known).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate nouns formed by noun + noun in objective relation (rule start)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenate, as a rule, nouns formed by the combination of two nouns standing in objective relation to each other—that is, one of whose components is derived from a transitive verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule is introduced and examples follow in subsequent text (text cut off in this chunk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling compounding: 'today', 'tomorrow', 'tonight', 'cannot', and spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Make one word of 'today,' 'tomorrow,' 'tonight,' 'cannot' (see rule 204). Distinguish between 'sometimes' and 'some time(s)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit guidance to prefer closed compounds for these common adverbs/constructions; see cross-reference to later rule for further details.
